title: How do you separate CI and CD pipelines in Jenkins (triggers at each stage), and how is Jenkins integrated with a Kubernetes cluster (agents as pods, Kubernetes plugin)?
shortTitle: Separating CI and CD Pipelines in Jenkins and Integrating Jenkins with Kubernetes

s1_definition.profdef: In Jenkins, separating CI from CD means running two distinct pipelines with different triggers: a CI pipeline triggered automatically on every push or pull request that builds, tests, scans, and publishes an immutable artifact, and a CD pipeline triggered by the successful completion of CI (or by a tag, or by a manual promotion) that takes that already-built artifact and deploys it to an environment. Jenkins integrates with Kubernetes through the Kubernetes plugin, which runs build agents as ephemeral pods inside the cluster: when a job starts, Jenkins asks the Kubernetes API to create a pod with the required tool containers, the build runs inside that pod, and the pod is destroyed afterward, giving clean, isolated, horizontally scalable build capacity.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank of India having two separate assembly lines. The first line (CI) takes raw cheque forms, checks them, and seals them into certified envelopes — it runs automatically every time a form arrives. The second line (CD) takes only certified envelopes and delivers them to the right branch — it only starts when the first line hands over a certified envelope, and for the main vault it waits for a manager's signature. For staffing, instead of keeping a hall full of permanent clerks sitting idle, the bank hires temporary clerks on demand: each cheque batch gets its own clerk who appears, does the work, and leaves. In Jenkins-on-Kubernetes terms, each build gets its own pod that spins up, runs the job, and disappears.
s1_definition.oneliner: CI builds and certifies an artifact on every push, CD deploys that same artifact when CI passes, and Jenkins runs each build in a throwaway Kubernetes pod.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In Jenkins, separating CI from CD means running two distinct pipelines with different triggers: a CI pipeline triggered automatically on every push or pull request that builds, tests, scans, and publishes an immutable artifact, and a CD pipeline triggered by the successful completion of CI (or by a tag, or by a manual promotion) that takes that already-built artifact and deploys it to an environment. Jenkins integrates with Kubernetes through the Kubernetes plugin, which runs build agents as ephemeral pods inside the cluster: when a job starts, Jenkins asks the Kubernetes API to create a pod with the required tool containers, the build runs inside that pod, and the pod is destroyed afterward, giving clean, isolated, horizontally scalable build capacity.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the National Bank of India having two separate assembly lines. The first line (CI) takes raw cheque forms, checks them, and seals them into certified envelopes — it runs automatically every time a form arrives. The second line (CD) takes only certified envelopes and delivers them to the right branch — it only starts when the first line hands over a certified envelope, and for the main vault it waits for a manager's signature. For staffing, instead of keeping a hall full of permanent clerks sitting idle, the bank hires temporary clerks on demand: each cheque batch gets its own clerk who appears, does the work, and leaves. In Jenkins-on-Kubernetes terms, each build gets its own pod that spins up, runs the job, and disappears.

**One line to remember:** CI builds and certifies an artifact on every push, CD deploys that same artifact when CI passes, and Jenkins runs each build in a throwaway Kubernetes pod.

sections.s2_technical:
Separating the two pipelines starts with triggers. The CI pipeline is defined in a `Jenkinsfile` and triggered by a source event. With the GitHub or GitLab plugin this is a webhook on push and pull request, configured with `triggers { githubPush() }` or by the multibranch pipeline scanning branches. Its job is to build, run tests, scan, and on success publish an artifact to a registry or repository manager, tagged with the commit. It must never deploy to an environment; its only output is a trustworthy artifact.

The CD pipeline is a separate job triggered by the CI result. A common way is the `build` step: at the end of CI you call `build job: 'transfer-service-cd', parameters: [string(name: 'IMAGE_TAG', value: env.GIT_COMMIT)]`, passing the exact artifact tag forward. Alternatively CD is triggered by a Git tag push for releases, or started manually by an operator who picks which already-built artifact to promote. Because CD receives a tag and never rebuilds, the thing tested in CI is exactly the thing deployed.

Environment promotion lives inside the CD pipeline as ordered stages with gates. A typical flow deploys to dev automatically, then to QA automatically, then pauses with an `input` step for human approval before production: `stage('Prod') { steps { input message: 'Deploy to production?', submitter: 'release-managers' }; ... }`. The `submitter` restricts who may approve, which in banking maps to a named release manager.

The Kubernetes integration is configured through the Kubernetes plugin on the Jenkins controller. You point Jenkins at the cluster API server and a namespace, and define a pod template. When a pipeline requests an agent with that label, Jenkins calls the Kubernetes API to create a pod. The pod usually has several containers: a JNLP container that talks back to the Jenkins controller, plus tool containers such as a Maven container to build and a Docker or Kaniko container to build images. The declarative syntax uses a `kubernetes` agent with a YAML pod spec.

Running agents as pods gives three big benefits. First, isolation: each build runs in a fresh pod with no leftover state from a previous build, which prevents one banking service's build from contaminating another. Second, elastic scale: if ten pull requests land at once, Jenkins asks Kubernetes for ten pods and they run in parallel, then the pods are destroyed, so you are not paying for idle agents. Third, consistency: the pod template pins exact tool versions, so every build uses the same Maven and JDK, removing the classic "works on my agent" problem.

A senior nuance is image building inside a pod. Mounting the host Docker socket is a security risk on a shared banking cluster because it gives the build root-equivalent access to the node. The safer pattern is Kaniko or Buildah, which build images in userspace without a Docker daemon, so a compromised build cannot take over the node. Another nuance is credentials: CD needs cluster deploy credentials and registry credentials, and these must come from Jenkins credential store or a secret manager injected at runtime, never baked into the Jenkinsfile.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India the team originally had one giant pipeline that built and deployed in a single run. When Priya just wanted to redeploy a known-good build to QA, she had to rebuild from scratch, which took twenty minutes and risked producing a slightly different artifact if a dependency had moved. This is exactly the problem CI/CD separation solves. CI produces one immutable artifact once; CD simply promotes that existing artifact, so redeploying is fast and byte-for-byte identical.

Problem 2 — The old pipeline ran on two permanent build servers. During a busy release day, ten merges queued up behind each other because only two builds could run at once, and the next morning those same servers sat idle wasting money. This is exactly the problem Jenkins-on-Kubernetes solves. Each build gets its own pod on demand, ten builds run in parallel across the cluster, and when the rush is over the pods vanish so nothing sits idle.

Problem 3 — A production incident happened when someone deployed straight to the live ledger with no approval. This is exactly the problem a CD approval gate solves. The CD pipeline deploys to dev and QA automatically, but pauses at an input step before production that only a named release manager can approve.

To make this concrete without a live Jenkins cluster, we will write a small Java simulation. We will model a `CiPipeline` that produces an immutable `Artifact` (an image tag) on a push event, and a `CdPipeline` that consumes an `Artifact` and promotes it through dev, QA, and production, pausing for approval before production. We will model build capacity with an `AgentPool` that represents Kubernetes pods created on demand and released after use. We will run a healthy push that builds an artifact and promotes it, showing the approval gate holding production until a release manager approves. This mirrors the real two-pipeline, pod-per-build design.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a push of commit `a1b2c3d4` for the transfer service, plus two attempts to promote the resulting artifact to production, one by an unauthorised developer and one by an authorised release manager.

Step 1: The push triggers CI. The AgentPool creates a pod `jenkins-agent-ci-1`, representing Jenkins asking Kubernetes for a build pod. The data is still just a commit identifier.

Step 2: Inside that pod, CI compiles, runs tests, and scans. It then constructs an immutable Artifact whose image tag is `registry.bank.local/transfer-service:a1b2c3d4`. The commit has now become a concrete, tagged artifact.

Step 3: CI finishes and the pod is released, representing Kubernetes destroying the build pod so nothing sits idle. The artifact survives because it was published to the registry.

Step 4: CD starts for the first promotion attempt. A new pod `jenkins-agent-cd-1` is created. CD deploys the same artifact to dev and QA automatically, changing the deployed image in those namespaces while the artifact itself stays identical.

Step 5: CD reaches the production approval gate. The approver is `rajesh-dev`, who is not in the release managers set, so the gate denies approval. Production is not touched and CD returns failure. The pod is released.

Step 6: CD starts again for the second attempt with approver `priya-release-mgr`. It redeploys the same artifact to dev and QA, reaches the gate, and this time the approver is authorised, so the gate approves and CD deploys the identical artifact to production.

sections.s6_takeaway:
In Jenkins I keep continuous integration and continuous delivery as two separate pipelines with different triggers. The CI pipeline is triggered automatically by a push or pull request webhook. Its only responsibility is to build, run unit and integration tests, run static analysis and vulnerability scans, and on success publish a single immutable artifact, usually a container image tagged with the commit SHA, to a registry. It must never deploy to an environment. The CD pipeline is triggered by CI success, typically with a post-success build step that passes the image tag forward, or by a release tag. Its only responsibility is to take that already-built artifact and promote it, so what was tested is exactly what is deployed, and redeploying to any environment is fast and byte-for-byte identical.

Inside the CD pipeline I model environment promotion as ordered stages with gates. Dev and QA deploy automatically, and production sits behind an input approval step restricted by submitter to named release managers. In banking that gate is essential, because a regulator expects a specific person to authorise any change to the live ledger, and the submitter restriction means only a release manager, not any developer, can approve.

For build capacity I integrate Jenkins with Kubernetes using the Kubernetes plugin. Instead of permanent build servers, each job requests an ephemeral agent pod. Jenkins calls the Kubernetes API, a pod is created with the exact tool containers it needs such as Maven and Kaniko, the build runs inside that pod, and the pod is destroyed afterward. This gives clean isolation so builds never contaminate each other, elastic parallelism so a rush of ten merges simply spins up ten pods, and pinned tool versions so there is no "works on my agent" drift.

On the banking project I ran exactly this setup for the transfer service. CI built and published an image tagged with the commit, CD promoted that image through dev, QA, and production with a release-manager approval before production, and every build ran in a throwaway pod. The senior point I always add is that I use Kaniko rather than mounting the host Docker socket, because mounting the socket on a shared cluster gives a build node-level root access, which is unacceptable for a system handling real money. Credentials for the cluster and registry come from the Jenkins credential store or Vault and are injected at runtime, never written into the Jenkinsfile.
